newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drug certification questioned by experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drug certification questioned by experts.

text.p: The annual U.S. certification of how effectively other countries fight drug-trafficking is drawing fire from foreign governments and experts who say the policy poisons international cooperation.

The U.S. State Department defended the system as a strong diplomatic tool and a few U.S. lawmakers are considering giving the policy more clout by instituting automatic trade sanctions for countries that repeatedly fail the test.

"The certification process has proved to be a remarkably effective diplomatic instrument for keeping all governments aware of the need to pull their weight in the international drug effort," the State Department's international narcotics control strategy report said.

The process, which has been in force since 1986, requires that the United States scrutinise major drug producing and transit countries to check whether they cooperated with Washington in fighting traffickers or took steps to meet their obligations under a 1988 U.N. Drug Convention.
Governments that do not pass muster are cut off from most U.S. aid and face Washington's negative vote when they request loans from development institutions like the World Bank.

The Clinton administration on Friday certified Mexico as a trustworthy ally despite overwhelming evidence of high-level corruption in the Mexican government but decertified Colombia, a much lesser U.S. trade partner, for a second year in a row.
Five other countries were put on the U.S. drug blacklist: Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria.
Foreign officials complain that it is ironic that the United States, the world's top drug-consuming nation, should judge others.
The United States has 12 million drug users, among them 3.6 million addicts, who use $50 billion worth of drugs a year, nearly half the world's illegal drugs.

Congressman Charles Rangel, a New York Democrat who voted for the original bill, believes the policy should be scrapped, saying that while some governments are disqualified for legitimate reasons, others are routinely thrown on the blacklist just because Washington considers them rogue states.
"If a friend does something bad, or something you don't agree with, you don't go and shoot him in the kneecaps," he said.
In less colourful terms, an expert panel sponsored by the Council on Foreign Affairs came to similar conclusions.

The group of former diplomats and law enforcement officials, economists, business leaders and human rights experts urged the United States to shift its drug policy away from its focus on reducing supply abroad to one that concentrates more on bringing down demand at home.
The experts noted that cocaine and heroin are cheaper, more potent and more available now even though Washington has spent $25 billion since 1981 on international drug control.
The panel concluded that certification is "a corrosive force in U.S.-Latin American relations" and called for an end to the unilateral inquisitions.

In private, some State Department officials admit that they have grown somewhat cynical about the process but predict it will survive because politicians enjoy playing diplomatic hardball with the drug issue.
While acknowledging that it is not a one-size-fits-all solution, they can also point out cases in which it has prodded countries into action.

In the latest round, for instance, Colombia said it passed more anti-drug legislation in the past few months than it did in the previous decade. Paraguay replaced its drug czar with an official trusted by Washington.
And several countries in Latin America and Eastern Europe pledged to establish mechanisms against money laundering for fear of being cut off from the U.S. banking system.
But even true believers were rankled by Clinton's call to certify Mexico.

Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman Jesse Helms blasted Mexico's certification as a fraud, arguing that Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo's government is as corrupt, if not more so, than the government of Colombian President Ernesto Samper.
